subject: art-design
promptStrong: Give me an exam-style {board} {level} {subject} question on {lo}, then mark my answer against the mark scheme.
promptWeak: Explain {lo} for {board} {level} {subject} simply, with a clear example and the most common mistake students make.

questions.q: What does the aperture setting on a camera primarily control?
options: The amount of light entering the lens and the depth of field
The colour temperature of the image
The number of pixels captured by the sensor
The file format the photo is saved in
questions.explain: Aperture (measured in f-stops) governs both how much light reaches the sensor and how much of the scene appears in sharp focus.

questions.q: The 'rule of thirds' is a compositional guide that involves:
options: Dividing the frame into a 3x3 grid and placing key elements along the lines or intersections
Using only three colours in an image
Taking three photographs of every subject
Setting the shutter speed to one third of a second
questions.explain: The rule of thirds splits the frame with two horizontal and two vertical lines, and placing subjects on these lines or their intersections creates a more balanced composition.

questions.q: A photographer wants a portrait with a sharply focused face and a soft, blurred background. Which setting best achieves this?
options: A wide aperture such as f/2.8 (shallow depth of field)
A narrow aperture such as f/22 (deep depth of field)
A very fast shutter speed
A very low ISO
questions.explain: A wide aperture (low f-number) produces a shallow depth of field, keeping the subject sharp while blurring the background.

questions.q: To freeze the exact moment a sprinter crosses the finish line without any blur, a photographer should use:
options: A fast shutter speed
A slow shutter speed
A wide aperture
A high ISO with a slow shutter
questions.explain: A fast shutter speed exposes the sensor for a very short time, freezing rapid motion sharply.

questions.q: What is a likely consequence of raising the ISO to a very high value in low light?
options: The image becomes more sensitive to light but shows more noise or grain
The image loses all its colour
The aperture automatically closes
The photo is saved as a RAW file
questions.explain: A higher ISO increases the sensor's sensitivity, allowing shooting in dim light but introducing visible noise or grain.

questions.q: Why might a photographer include strong 'leading lines' such as a road or fence in a composition?
options: To guide the viewer's eye towards the main subject or focal point
To increase the resolution of the image
To reduce the depth of field
To change the white balance
questions.explain: Leading lines draw the viewer's gaze through the frame and direct attention to the intended focal point.

questions.q: A student wants to photograph a waterfall so the water appears as a smooth, silky blur. Which technique is most appropriate?
options: A slow shutter speed, ideally with the camera on a tripod
A fast shutter speed handheld
A wide aperture with a fast shutter
The highest possible ISO
questions.explain: A slow shutter speed captures the water's movement over time as a soft blur, and a tripod keeps the surroundings sharp.

questions.q: Which file format stores minimally processed data straight from the camera sensor, giving the most flexibility when editing?
options: RAW
JPEG
GIF
PDF
questions.explain: A RAW file holds unprocessed sensor data, allowing greater control over exposure, white balance and detail during editing.

questions.q: The JPEG file format is best described as:
options: A compressed format that loses some image data to reduce file size
A lossless format that keeps every pixel unchanged
A format that cannot be opened in editing software
A vector-based format
questions.explain: JPEG uses lossy compression, discarding some data to create smaller files at the cost of image quality.

questions.q: What is the main advantage of using layers in software such as Adobe Photoshop?
options: Different elements and edits can be worked on separately without permanently altering the original image
It automatically increases the camera's aperture
It converts colour photographs into RAW files
It removes the need to save the file
questions.explain: Layers allow non-destructive editing, so adjustments and elements can be changed or removed independently.

questions.q: A photographer wants to remove a small blemish and an unwanted litter bin from an otherwise perfect photo. Which tools are most suitable?
options: The clone stamp and healing tools
The crop tool only
The saturation slider
The white balance selector
questions.explain: Clone stamp and healing tools sample nearby pixels to cover unwanted marks or objects seamlessly.

questions.q: Why does a low-resolution image often look blurry or blocky when printed large?
options: It contains too few pixels to hold detail at a bigger size
It has too many layers
It was saved in RAW format
Its aperture was set too wide
questions.explain: Resolution is measured in pixels, and too few pixels spread over a large print makes individual pixels visible as blur or blockiness.

questions.q: Increasing the 'saturation' of a digital image will:
options: Make the colours appear more intense and vivid
Sharpen the edges of objects
Reduce the file size
Increase the depth of field
questions.explain: Saturation controls the intensity or purity of colour, so raising it makes hues appear stronger and more vibrant.

questions.q: Ansel Adams is best known for which type of photography?
options: Black and white landscape photography and the Zone System
Colour fashion photography
Candid street photography
Underwater macro photography
questions.explain: Ansel Adams is famous for dramatic black and white landscapes and developed the Zone System for controlling tonal exposure.

questions.q: Henri Cartier-Bresson is closely associated with which idea and genre?
options: 'The decisive moment' and street photography
Staged studio portraiture
Large-scale digital collage
Colour advertising photography
questions.explain: Cartier-Bresson, a pioneer of candid street photography, coined 'the decisive moment' for capturing a scene at its most telling instant.

questions.q: Man Ray created images called 'rayographs'. What was distinctive about how these were made?
options: They were made without a camera, by placing objects directly onto light-sensitive paper
They were the first colour photographs
They were taken using very long exposures at night
They were composed entirely of text
questions.explain: A rayograph (photogram) is produced by laying objects on photographic paper and exposing it to light, needing no camera.

questions.q: Dorothea Lange, famous for the image 'Migrant Mother', is best described as a photographer working in which genre?
options: Documentary photography
Abstract photography
Fashion photography
Macro photography
questions.explain: Lange documented social conditions such as the Great Depression, and 'Migrant Mother' is an iconic documentary image.

questions.q: A student photographs unposed, candid moments of everyday life in a busy town market. Which genre does this work best fit?
options: Street photography
Still life photography
Studio portraiture
Architectural photography
questions.explain: Capturing spontaneous, unposed everyday life in public places is the defining feature of street photography.
